He went on to later say that there might be a reasonable case for preventing treating AI abusively, but not out of concern for its interests, but instead out of concern that being mean to it might make us cruel.

item.title: Pangram Works. Deal With It.
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

A common belief is that AI detectors don’t work. It’s weird that this view has stuck around because it’s demonstrably false. It’s true that a lot of AI detectors are junk. But Pangram works extremely well. It is highly reliable. If Pangram flags your writing as AI, odds are very good that it is.

How do we know that Pangram works? Pangram claims to have a false positive rate that is extremely low, being negligible everywhere but in a few niche areas. And that was in 2025; accuracy has gone up since then.

Other reviews find similarly. A collaboration between Pangram and University of Maryland researchers found Pangram has “a false positive rate of 0.0041% and a false negative rate of 0.3396%.” While Pangram is less reliable for short snippets of text, it is still pretty reliable. And the high accuracy of Pangram has been confirmed by various other studies.

Pangram is so good that it’s almost impossible to produce an example of it being wrong. Someone named Nition on Twitter offered people $500 if they could find a text of at least 750 consecutive words, written prior to 2019, that Pangram flagged as more than 75% AI-written. Eventually someone cracked it, but it took several weeks, and the text in question was a deeply weird poem that repeated “the next night we ate whale,” for most of the poem.

I’ve witnessed people over and over again claim to have counterexamples to Pangram only for it to turn out that the text in question really is AI-generated or that they’ve pulled some shenanigans. For instance, in one case, I saw a person literally doctor a screenshot to make it look like Pangram falsely flagged something as AI-generated when it wasn’t. If Pangram wasn’t highly reliable, people wouldn’t need to resort to such bizarre antics.

I basically think this is a pretty open and shut case. That Pangram works is a testable empirical matter. It’s been tested. It does work. There’s no longer room for debate. So what do the Pangram critics say? Mostly kind of crazy stuff. For example, one person suggested that the prize for people who could find counterexamples to Pangram was racist!

What in the world?

Emily Bender, whose main writing beat is performing mental gymnastics extreme enough to be the envy of the world’s leading gymnasts, in support of the conclusion that AI is useless junk, wrote an essay titled Pangram is not an oracle. She writes:

To get a sense of how well a language processing system is working, you need to look at both the false negative rate and the false positive rate. Looking at just overall accuracy could be misleading—it will depend heavily on the true positive rate in the test data. Similarly, looking at just false positives or false negatives is also misleading, because there is always a trade-off. Want something that has no false negatives? Design the system to always return “synthetic”. Want no false positives? Always return “authentic”.

Yes, that is obviously true, but Pangram has both low false positive AND false negative rates. Bender then writes, bizarrely:

Obviously to know your AI detector is useful, you need to know that it has a low rate of false positives and false negatives. That is why Pangram discusses the low rates of both in different places. Now, is it misleading to in some places only talk about one of them? No, obviously not, because each one carries useful information. If you want to figure out the probability that a piece flagged as AI is AI, you need only be concerned with the false positive rate. If you want to figure out the probability that a piece flagged as not being AI is AI, you only need to know the false negative rate.1

Bender then says “Regardless, before anyone uses Pangram for any specific use case, they need to be able to judge if it was actually evaluated with sufficiently similar language use.” But Pangram has been found to be highly reliable across many different kinds of texts. The only kinds it’s unreliable for are weird and niche. So then you can use induction to figure out how reliable it is for a kind of text whose genre you haven’t looked at accuracy scores for. If you notice that Pangram is near flawless for news articles, movie scripts, books, recipes, medical papers, congressional transcripts, and even Japanese Wikipedia articles, then you should assume that it’s also reliable in whatever domain you’re concerned about.

It is remarkable that in a piece intending to argue against using Pangram, Bender presents no empirical evidence about its accuracy. Surely that is relevant. Surely we cannot divine a priori the accuracy of Pangram! When pointed this out in a back-and-forth with Timnit Gebru, compadre of Bender, Gebru replied:

If Pangram is unreliable, just present the evidence for that! Why can nobody do this? Why is the response from the Pangram haters to raise the problem of induction??? It makes even less sense when you consider that Pangram’s accuracy has been verified across almost every conceivable kind of text.

I’ve been pretty astonished by the accuracy of Pangram. When I tried to fool Pangram by writing in a maximally AI-like way, I was able to do it, but it was difficult, and I kept having to go back and revise. I couldn’t even get it to say that the text was wholly AI unless it was pretty short. When I plugged a YouTube script into Pangram that struck me as likely largely but not entirely AI-generated, Pangram came back with a declaration that it was 60ish% AI. It works even though I pasted it with the timestamps and all.

Now, the correct view about Pangram is more nuanced than “it’s an infallible oracle for divining the precise portion of text that is AI-generated.” It sometimes fails for short snippets of text, particularly bizarrely repetitive text (like the whale text), and the percentage of the text it flags as AI-generated isn’t always the exact percentage that is. But overall, it’s quite reliable. If it says your article is AI-generated, odds are very good that it is.

Why does Pangram have so many haters? I think there are three main reasons. First, Pangram is AI. So lots of the instinctive AI haters don’t like Pangram. This is why Bender and Gebru have such opposition to it. Second, people conflate it with other AI detectors that are much less reliable. Third, lots of people use AI to write for them—if you do this, Pangram will identify it. Pangram is hated because it works.

1

Well, plus the prior, but that’s not the kind of thing that you could have general reliable data on.

item.title: Donation Matching Plus Horrifying Undercover Report
item.description: How you can help lots of animals
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

Important article, so please Restack and share.

Recently, the Humane League UK carried out an undercover investigation on UK chicken farms. What they found was horrifying.

Most UK chickens belong to fast-growing breeds, meaning they become huge extremely fast. This causes a range of serious health conditions. The video above shows footage of dead birds next to the living. Birds struggled to support their own weight given their huge size.

The ground was saturated with waste, leading to ammonia burning the skin of chickens. I highly recommend watching the video. I also recommend reading about ’s story, who, alongside several others, rescued two goats that he said were in dire conditions people, and faced serious legal consequences. I admire the bravery of those who go undercover to document those horrors, even at major personal risk.

If you want to do something about this—and other horrendous suffering—fortunately you can. Animal Charity Evaluators is currently doing donation matching. ACE evaluates animal charities to find the most effective ones. By donating, you can help fund these highly effective recommended charities. The best animal charities help multiple animals per dollar—in many cases stopping animals from suffering for many years in a cage per dollar they receive.

So please, if you can, donate to spare incomprehensible numbers of animals from horrendous agony.

item.title: Evolutionary Debunking Debunking
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

The evolutionary debunking argument is probably the best argument for moral anti-realism.

Moral realism is the idea that there are objective moral facts—facts about what’s wrong or right, good or bad, that don’t depend on anyone’s attitudes. Moral anti-realism is the idea that moral realism ain’t true. Moral realists think it’s wrong to torture babies and this fact doesn’t intrinsically depend on anyone’s attitude about it. Even if the whole world thought torturing babies was fine, it would still be wrong.1

The central argument for moral realism is that it’s the intuitive view. It seems very obvious that torturing babies for fun is wrong, and this fact doesn’t depend on what people think about it. That I or my culture disapproves of boiling babies or being pointlessly cruel to people isn’t part of why it’s wrong. In general, you should believe things that seem obvious when you think about them.

That is why, even before hearing the proof, you should think that in non-curved space the shortest distance between two points is a straight line, that the inside of relation is transitive, and that simpler hypotheses are likelier than more complex ones. You believe these because they appear obvious when you think about them. For similar reasons, you should believe moral realism.

The evolutionary debunking argument is a response to that core argument. The basic idea is that we don’t need to invoke moral facts to explain our moral intuitions. Instead, we can explain them evolutionarily. Moral beliefs would be likely to evolve, even if they weren’t accurate, because they’re adaptive. They help facilitate cooperation. Thus, because we’d have moral beliefs whether or not there were moral facts, we shouldn’t treat our moral beliefs as confirming that there are moral facts.

As I say, I think this is a very interesting argument. But I don’t ultimately think that it’s right. The things I say are similar to what Justin Clark-Doane argues in an influential paper—read it, it’s an absolute banger.

It isn’t always true that an evolutionary explanation of a belief undermines it. Evolution explains why you think there’s a table in front of you. But this doesn’t mean you shouldn’t think there’s a table. This is because evolution selects for accurate beliefs about tables.

If it appears to you that there’s some entity, there’s no reason to think the entity really exists so long as there isn’t an explanatory link between the entity and the appearance. If evolution selected for creatures who thought that in Andromeda there was a turquoise balloon, your intuition about the balloon would give you no reason to think it existed, because the existence of the balloon wouldn’t explain our beliefs about it. In contrast, your belief that there’s a table in front of you isn’t debunked by evolution, because it’s explained by the fact that there really is a table in front of you.

So then the evolutionary debunking argument is dependent on the success of a different argument for moral anti-realism. This argument goes:

  1. For our moral beliefs to be justified, the moral facts must explain our moral beliefs.

  2. The moral facts don’t explain our moral beliefs.

  3. Therefore, our moral beliefs aren’t justified.

I think the standard evolutionary debunking arguments works only if this argument works. But does it?

I agree that it’s puzzling how the moral facts might explain our moral beliefs. But I don’t think this can be an argument specifically against moral realism, because it would prove too much. To see this, consider four analogues:

  1. Logical beliefs: these are beliefs like that modus ponens is necessarily valid.

  2. Mathematical beliefs: for example, that there’s no largest integer. While maybe some arithmatical beliefs are only adaptive if they’re true, others, like the consistency of the Peano axioms, don’t derive their evolutionary functionality from their truth.

  3. Modal beliefs: these are beliefs about what’s possible and necessary—for example, married bachelors are impossible. It’s not just that they don’t exist, they couldn’t exist!

  4. Priors: these are beliefs about which states of affairs are intrinsically likelier than which others. For example, the intrinsic probability of a world that started in the state our world was at during the Big Bang is greater than one that started in the state our world was at five minutes ago. Similarly, a world where the laws are uniform is more likely than one where the laws of nature will be totally different one second from now.

It is equally puzzling how we know each of these things. How could facts about intrinsic probability explain our beliefs about intrinsic probability? The fact that some state of affairs is intrinsically likelier than another isn’t the kind of thing that can move around atoms. So it can’t explain our beliefs (or so it would seem). And it won’t do to give up these as genuine sources of knowledge, because without the fourth category, you can’t know that evolution happened—you can’t even know the world is more than five minutes old! There are an infinite number of theories that fit the data. If you don’t trust intuitions about intrinsic likelihood, then you have no way of knowing which one to pick.

Exactly where things go wrong is a bit less clear. There are three basic approaches. First, you can argue that God gives us a direct faculty for grasping these kinds of truths. That’s my preferred route. Second, you can try to give some naturalistic explanation of how the facts in these domains explain our beliefs about them. I’m skeptical that this works, but it’s an option. Third, you can loosen the explanatory requirement on belief; you can think that these cases illustrate that you can have beliefs based on intuitions without there being an explanatory connection between the belief and the intuition.

None of these seem that promising on their own. But one of them has to be right, because otherwise we’d have no mathematical, modal, and priors-based knowledge.

Now, obviously there’s a lot more to say here. But this is my basic sense of the lay of the land. Morality survives evolutionary debunking, because evolutionary debunking only works if you assume that the moral facts don’t explain our moral beliefs. But that proves too much, because a similar argument would rule out many other kinds of perfectly ordinary knowledge.

1

Anti-realist accounts can generally affirm that sentence as literally construed, though it’s unclear whether they live up to the spirit of it or if, to use the technical term, they’re just trying to cheese you.

item.title: The Era of Human Mathematicians is Over
item.description: AI has (very likely) solved one of the biggest unsolved problems in math
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

AI has (very likely) solved the Riemann hypothesis. This is unbelievably big news. It means, in some sense, that the era of the human mathematician is over.

I’m not a mathematician. But talk to your friendly neighborhood mathematician if you want to get a sense of how big of a deal this is. The Riemann hypothesis’s Wikipedia page says “Many consider it to be the most important unsolved problem in pure mathematics.” Terence Tao suggested about a month ago that it might be solved by 2050. There’s a million dollar prize for solving it.

And it was just solved. Or, well, probably it was. The prediction markets have the odds around 96% that at least one additional Millenium prize problem was solved. This was at 20% before the announcement, so it’s basically all based on confidence in the recent proof.1

It was reportedly solved by a human mathematician named Levent Alpöge who works for Anthropic and got the proof by repeatedly prompting Claude. It was formalized in Lean which double checks to make sure proofs are sound. While Lean isn’t infallible, it is a pretty strong indicator of reliability, and no issues have been found yet.

Probably I’m not the best guy to explain the Riemann hypothesis, but sure, whatever, I’ll try (after some discussion with Claude). Prime numbers get rarer and rarer. There are various formulas for estimating the number of primes up to some number. However, these formulas only approximate the number of primes—there’s some remaining margin of error. Riemann found a function whose zeroes—the points where it equals zero—tell you the possible margins for error.

The inputs to that function are points on a plane. The Riemann hypothesis is the idea that all those zeroes (or at least, all the interesting ones—there are some that sit at -2, -4, -6, -8 etc off to the left forever) all lie at an x value of 1/2. If this is right, it implies that the margins for error are as small as they could possibly be. The proof is of the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which entails the Riemann hypothesis as a special case.

Who cares?

Answer: mathematicians.

Why?

Because it’s relevant to a huge number of important areas in math. The “consequences” section on the Wikipedia page has seven subsections. My mathematician friend Mark tells me that a huge number of other proofs depend on the Riemann hypothesis. A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is thus a proof of many things. My guess is that many mathematicians would have regarded a proof of the Riemann hypothesis as the most significant proof that one could give.

There is some important sense in which this means the era of the human mathematician is over. If AI can prove the Riemann hypothesis, it can prove most any theorem that a mathematician could prove. Nearly all future mathematical progress will be driven by AIs. The prevailing view before the proof was that proving the Riemann hypothesis would be much harder than proving lots of other unsolved theorems. If AI can crack the Riemann hypothesis, many other theorems will soon follow.

To get a sense for how huge this is, imagine that AI made a brand new invention that humans had been working on for a long time. Maybe it figured out how to get efficient nuclear fusion. Maybe it figured out the theory of everything in physics. Maybe in philosophy it found such strong arguments that they definitively shut the door on lots of unsolved philosophical problems.

This is what has happened to mathematics. The era of the human mathematician is over. My guess is 2026 will be the last year when most mathematical discoveries were made by humans. And it isn’t even true that the most important mathematical discoveries were made by humans this year. There will be some period, like in chess, when AI-human teams do better than AIs alone. At some point, this period will be end, and it will be the age of the machines.

My guess is this will soon happen in other disciplines. It is not just the mathematician who will be rendered obsolete. It is every area of intellectual activity. Soon it will come for biology, and physics, and philosophy. It wouldn’t surprise me if next year AI proves some extremely cool impossibility results in population ethics.

This is a cause both for excitement and alarm. Excitement because it means we’re going to learn a bunch of amazingly cool non-obvious things. Alarm because it means AI models are very powerful, we are near superintelligence, and this makes them very dangerous. Burying our heads in the sand will not make AI capabilities go away. Pretending they’re useless stochastic parrots wasn’t plausible two years ago, and at this point is completely delusional.

I’ll close with some words from Scott Aaronson:

The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy. But for how much longer? For how much longer will anything last that we currently take for granted?

1

Weirdly, someone else later the same day claimed to have a proof, but that’s not what swung the prediction markets.

item.title: The Very Repugnant is Correct
item.description: Is the very repugnant conclusion a very repugnant conclusion?
item.content:encoded:
By Bentham's Bulldog

*This post is heavily indebted to a session Jake Nebel led, with a very helpful handout, in the ethics seminar he co-teaches with Liz Harman.

After making Adam, God cast him from paradise. After making his monster, Frankenstein cast him aside. When Derek Parfit proved the repugnant conclusion, he quaked before his invention—and spurned and burned what he had birthed. And when Arrhenius proved the very repugnant conclusion, he declared it a horrendous paradox—perhaps even a reason for moral skepticism—rather than a proof.

The very repugnant conclusion is the idea that a world with 10 billion people with great lives is less good than a world with tons of people with terrible lives and an astronomical number of people with lives barely worth living.1 Totalism, the view that I think is right, says the value of the world is determined by summing together everyone’s welfare. Totalism implies the very repugnant conclusion—if there are enough people with lives barely worth living, they can bump up the total to be higher than the total in the world of 10 billion people with very happy lives.

In the above graph, A depicts a population of a bunch of people with great lives. B depicts a population with a bunch of people with terrible lives and then an even more numerous bunch of people with barely worthwhile lives. The very repugnant conclusion is the idea that B>A.

The problem for those who don’t accept the VRC is that it’s extremely hard to avoid. Arrhenius proved it from a few very modest axioms, each of which seem extremely obvious when you think about them (read here for a great explainer, though I’m going to attempt to explain his most significant proof). Other strong arguments for accepting it abound.

People hate the VRC. They hate it so much that after Arrhenius produced some of his proofs, he wrote “the impossibility theorem cast doubts on the whole project of finding a normative theory that coheres with our considered moral beliefs.” Even Chat-GPT doesn’t like the very repugnant conclusion, so much so that it won’t draw me a graph of it. That’s why I had to draw the above graph by hand! Surely, whatever you think about it, it’s not that repugnant.

In this article, I’m not going to canvass every argument for accepting the very repugnant conclusion. The best one is probably the Arrhenius proof, which I’ll give a slightly simplified version of. This version has a tiny bit less force than the original, but still almost all of the force while being significantly simpler.

A brief note on names: I think it’s a bit unfair that the conclusions were given such charged names. The view that every totalist is straightforwardly committed to gets the name “the very repugnant conclusion.” Lance Bush voice: very repugnant to whom? Certainly it’s not very repugnant to me.

And one of the other results that views have is the “sadistic conclusion”—even though views that imply it aren’t sadistic. The views don’t like suffering. They just dislike suffering less than they dislike proliferating huge numbers of barely happy people. I think people would have less strong intuitions if the views in question weren’t given such charged names.

Trump voice: we’ve been treated so unfairly in terms of names, but that’s okay, right, we’re still winning by a lot—like nobody’s ever seen before!

Argument 1 Mom, can we have an Arrhenius proof? No, we have them at home. The impossibility proof at home.

This argument is Arrhenius-inspired but it’s not any of the Arrhenius proofs, I think, though I don’t know all of them off the top of my head—apologies if I’ve inadvertently plagiarized him. Also draws a bit from Huemer’s argument. Think of it as like if Arrhenius’s sixth proof and Huemer’s argument had a baby.

Start with a world with ten billion people with great lives. Now, imagine making one of those people a tiny bit worse off and creating a bunch of happy people. Seems like an improvement. Do that again. An improvement once more.

Keep doing that until all the original ten billion people have been made horribly badly off. At each step of the way things are getting better. So from this, we’ve learned that a world with ten billion people with great lives is less good than one with ten billion people with terrible lives and a huge number of people with great lives.

But now imagine raising everyone’s welfare level and flooding the world with a huge number of people with lives barely worth living. This seems like an improvement. So now we have the result that a world with a huge number of people with barely worthwhile lives, a bunch with great lives, and a bunch with horrible lives is better than one with a large number of great lives.

Now, imagine lowering the welfare of one of the people with great lives by a tiny amount to double the welfare of a thousand people with barely worthwhile lives. That’s an improvement. Do that again and again and again until all the people with great lives have been reduced to lives barely worth living. Once again, that’s an improvement. But once all the people with great lives are ground down to barely worthwhile lives, we’ve simply reproduced the very repugnant conclusion. And at each step of the way, things have gotten better.

Here’s a very fancy graph representing this, made by yours truly. The Y axis represents the amount of well-being of the people and the X axis represents the number of people.

W2>W1 because you get W2 by repeatedly slightly lowering the welfare of one person in the original group in W1 and creating a bunch of people with great lives. W3>W2 because everyone who exists in W2 is better off in W3 than W2—plus there are extra people with good lives.2 W3 is what you get when you raise everyone’s welfare in W2 and create a bunch of new people with lives barely worth living. W4>W3 because it’s what you get by repeatedly slightly lowering the welfare of one of the well-off people in W3 and doubling the welfare of a hundred people with lives barely worth living. W4>W1 just is the very repugnant conclusion.

W1, W2, W3, W4—you’re done, so figure out why you were wrong.

Argument 2 Parfit’s argument extended

Here’s a simple argument. Start with a group of ten billion people with great lives. Let’s say their welfare is all 100. Now, imagine raising their welfare all to 110 and creating 10 billion new people with welfare of 80. It seems that things have gotten better. Now, imagine a third world where all twenty billion people have a welfare level of 99. Things are better still. You can keep doing analogous things until you bring people down to having just barely worthwhile lives (more details in a footnote).3 From this we can derive that a world with a bunch of people with barely worthwhile lives is better than one with 10 billion people with great lives.

A similar argument shows that a world with a bunch of people with slightly bad lives is worse than one with 10 billion people with horrible lives. 10 billion people with welfare level -100 is less bad than 100 billion with welfare level -99 which is less bad than 1 trillion with welfare level -98…which is less bad than some huge number of people with welfare level -.1.

Now, imagine starting with a world with 10 billion people with great lives. Imagine then adding a huge number of people with great lives and one person with a slightly bad life. It seems that things have gotten better. Do that again and again and again, until there are a bunch of people with great lives and a bunch of people with slightly bad lives. Now, replace the set of people with great lives with a bunch of people with barely worthwhile lives—things have gotten better. Then replace the set of people with barely bad lives with a much smaller group with horrible lives. That is better, per the above argument. So, in the end, a bunch of people with miserable lives and a gargantuan number with lives barely worth living is better than one with a huge number with great lives.

Argument 3 The Arrhenius proof simplified

Technically what’s proved is the additive very repugnant conclusion: adding a population of a bunch of people with great lives is less good than adding a population of a bunch of people with horrible lives and a gargantuan number with lives barely worth living. I’m also going to simplify the proof a tiny bit, and modify things slightly—this only weakens the argument by a small amount but vastly increases ease of explanation. If you want to read the more complete version with its full force, see here. Think of what I’m presenting not as my own argument but as Arrhenius’s with a few shortcuts taken.

Here’s the basic idea of the proof. Start with a population of a bunch of people with barely worthwhile lives. Assume that the population size is really big. First, imagine adding 10 billion people with great lives to that world. The way the proof works is we’ll argue that the situation could be improved again and again and again, until it simply consists of adding a bunch of miserable people and a gargantuan number with barely worthwhile lives.

Now, imagine making one of the 10 billion people you’ve added slightly worse off to bring up a hundred other preexisting people to having great lives. Seems like it’s an improvement (or, at minimum, things aren’t worse). This follows from non-extreme priority which says that a world where one person has a slightly lower welfare level and a bunch of others have great lives is better than or equal to one where the one has a slightly higher welfare and the others have lives barely worth living. In other words, bringing up a bunch of people to high welfare is worth one person having a slightly lower welfare.

Now, make them worse off again and again and again, until they’re all horribly badly off. At each step, one of the ten billion is just slightly worse off and many others are brought up to a high welfare level. So, from this, we get the result that bumping up a bunch of people to have great lives is worth creating a bunch of people with horrible lives (negative utilitarianism BTFOd).

Now, weak non-sadism says that having a huge population with barely worthwhile lives is better than or equal to a smaller population of people with negative lives. More precisely, some number of lives at some sufficiently negative welfare are so bad that adding them is worse than adding any number of people at slightly positive welfare level.

So now imagine swapping out many of the people with horrible lives with a very large population of people with barely worthwhile lives. Once again, things are better. Though make sure to keep around some people with terrible lives.

Slightly stronger non-elitism4 says the following: suppose there are two welfare levels, x and y. x is more than y. If there’s a big enough group, it’s at least as good for all of the people to be at welfare level x as for one to be at welfare level x+1 and the rest to be at welfare level y. So, in other words, if x is more than y, in a large enough group, everyone at x is better than or equal to one person at x+1 and everyone else at y.

So now imagine lowering the welfare level of one person who currently has a great life to bump up a bunch of the people with barely worthwhile lives to be almost as good. That’s an improvement—or at the very least, not a worsening. Do that again and again and again until all the people with great lives have a slightly lower welfare level. Many with barely worthwhile lives have a much better life now, but there are still tons with barely worthwhile lives.

Repeat the process. Keep lowering one person’s welfare level to bump up a bunch of people to slightly lower welfare levels. At each step of the way, things are either as good or better. In the end, if you apply that enough times, you’re left with a population where everyone with a good life has a barely good life.

Now, imagine raising the welfare of everyone who didn’t originally exist—so everyone who wasn’t part of the original population has slightly better barely worth living lives. And we still had some left over people with terrible lives. So in the end, it’s better to add a population of people with barely worthwhile lives and many with terrible lives than a smaller population with great lives.

The reason we needed this last step was that the other steps are all consistent with each process leaving things equally good. This establishes that things are better, so that the world is better at the end, not just equally good.

I found the proof a bit hard to get a handle on at first, so here’s the basic idea. Basically, there are four substantive steps, starting from the population where 10 billion people with great lives were added:

  1. Make the super well off people miserable to bump up the people with barely worthwhile lives. This leaves things at least as good, per repeated applications of non-extreme priority.

  2. Replace most of the miserable people with a shit ton of people with barely worthwhile lives, but keep some miserable people left over. This leaves things at least as good, per weak non-sadism.

  3. Now, level everyone down to have just barely worthwhile lives. This is at least as good by non-elitism. Make sure to return the people who originally had barely worthwhile lives to their original level.

  4. Lastly, make the people who were created better off, so things are better in the end. This is better obviously.

We need one last premise which is that you can convert great lives to just barely worthwhile lives by repeatedly making them a bit worse (plus transitivity, but that’s not super needed, for reasons we’ll see later). More precisely “This assumption states that there exists a finite sequence of slight welfare differences between any two welfare levels.” Why think this?

The reason you might be tempted to deny this is if you think that the good life depends on organic unities. For example, maybe having a good life depends on valuable relationships and knowledge. But these properties are either had or lacked. So maybe the step where one loses a valuable relationship incurs a major loss in welfare. Perhaps there aren’t a series of small lowerings, but instead one giant fall.

This is a very interesting suggestion, but I don’t think it works for seven reasons.

First, goods like relationships can be reduced to goods of barely any value by a process of slow degradation. Imagine the person you have a relationship slowly being disposed to do fewer and fewer nicer things, until they barely care about you at all—until they’re just a bit more than an acquaintance.

Second, there’s a more straightforward way to lower the value of whichever goods are in a great life. Just lower the person’s degree of conscious experience, until it dwindles to almost non-existence—until they’re on the edge of zombiehood—and they’ll have a life barely worth living.

Third, for the proof we don’t quite need the assumption that any good life can be gradually degraded to a life that’s barely worth living. All we need is the assumption that there can be arbitrarily good lives that can be gradually degraded to a life that’s barely worth living. Here’s how that proof would work.

Suppose you think that the standard great human life can’t be degraded gradually in this way. Call degradable lives ones that can. If degradable lives can be arbitrarily good, then there’s a world full of degradable lives better than any one with 10 billion people with great lives. But then apply the steps in the proof to that life—and by transitivity, this implies the very repugnant conclusion.

Fourth, even if you think many great lives aren’t degradable, so long as some are, the very repugnant conclusion implies the very repugnant conclusion for some degradable lives. Suppose, for example, that you think pleasure and pain are degradable. This is very plausible because degree of pleasure can be slowly lowered and degree of pain can be slowly increased. The proof then will imply that a world full of arbitrarily pleasurable lives is less good than one with a bunch of people being tortured and a gargantuan number with barely worthwhile lives.

Fifth, even if you think that good lives aren’t degradable, the steps of the proof can be reconstructed with whatever kinds of lowerings you think are possible. So, for example, suppose you think that to make a great life into a barely-worthwhile life, you’d need to lower it by medium increments. Then, we’d modify non-extreme priority into saying that a world where one person has a lower welfare level by a medium amount and a bunch of others have great lives is better than or equal to one where the one has a mediumly higher welfare and the others have lives barely worth living. The steps will still seem very plausible.

Sixth, if you think welfare can be represented as a real number, then denying this step involves denying that people can have welfare levels corresponding to certain real numbers. This would be kind of weird in its own right. But even if it’s true, it seems that one could still accept the premises as being claims about counterpossibles. So if, counterpossibly, there were a person with a life slightly less good than the life of the person with a great life, moving the person with a great life down to that level would be worth bringing a bunch of people up to his level.

Seventh, as Elliott Thornley showed, there’s another similarish proof that doesn’t need that assumption.

Which other premise might a person reject? The one with the most extreme implications is non-elitism. But isn’t that one obvious when you think about it? Lowering one person by a tiny amount to bring up a huge number of people to a level just a bit below theirs doesn’t make things worse! Seems crazy to deny it.

If you deny it, then you must think that lowering the welfare of a super well-off person by a tiny amount wouldn’t worth bringing up any number of people to a slightly lower level. But is this plausible? Think about some super well-off person. Wouldn’t it be better if they were slightly less well-off, and everyone in the world with a life barely worth living was made almost as well-off as them?

How about weak non-sadism? That’s the one that seems most plausible to me to deny. Still, it’s not that plausible. It implies that creating a bunch of happy lizards would be worse than creating a smaller number of people being tortured. That can’t be! At the very least, this seems much more repugnant than the repugnant conclusion. More on that later.

The view also implies that creating happy lizards—or happy humans, with barely worthwhile lives—is bad instead of good. But that doesn’t seem right. The lizards like their lives. They want to live. Why not let them? I’ll talk more about this in section 7.

Argument 4 Many good things

Here is a very simple argument:

  1. A person existing with a good life is good.

  2. If there are infinite people who exist, their average goodness is above zero or infinitesimal.

  3. If there are infinity things whose average goodness is above zero or infinitesimal, then together there’s an infinite amount of good.

  4. Thus, an infinite number of people with barely worthwhile lives is infinitely good (if you don’t like infinities, you can run this argument with some other suitably large number, but I’m going to use infinities because it’s cleaner that way. But note: nothing about the argument depends on infinities).

  5. A bunch of people with horrible lives is very bad but not infinitely bad.

  6. If there is one infinitely good thing and one bad but not infinitely bad thing, together, they are infinitely good.

  7. Therefore, the world with infinite people with barely worthwhile lives and a bunch of miserable people is infinitely good.

  8. If 7, then the very repugnant conclusion is true.

  9. Therefore, the very repugnant conclusion is true.

Every premise seems pretty plausible! You might be tempted to reject 1. I’ll explain later why I don’t find that tenable. You might want to reject 2 if you think that the marginal value of adding a person with a barely good life declines. For example, maybe the first person with a barely good life has a value of 1, the next of .5, the next of .25, etc. But this implies that adding the first person is better than adding 10 quadrillion people after there are already a lot of people.

This is hard to believe. It doesn’t seem like the goodness of a person being created depends on how many other people there are. Learning there were a bunch of aliens with barely worthwhile lives wouldn’t affect the value of creating a person with a barely worthwhile life. And it certainly wouldn’t lower its value a trillion-fold.

Argument 5 How repugnant is the very repugnant conclusion?

Is the very repugnant conclusion even that repugnant?

I don’t think so. To see this, imagine there were a bunch of planets. On each one, there are two things you might learn:

  1. There is just one organism who is living a great life.

  2. There is one miserable organism and a trillion organisms with barely worthwhile lives.

It seems intuitively plausible that learning 2 is better news than learning 1. Finding one alien with a great life would be less good than finding a bunch of aliens with barely good lives and one with a bad life. But a world where 2 is true on every planet is full of people with miserable lives and a vastly larger number with barely worthwhile lives, while a world where 1 is true on every planet has a bunch of people with great lives. So if 2>1 on each planet, then the very repugnant conclusion is true.

Wouldn’t it be better to discover there’s a vast ecosystem of almost all barely happy animals, with a single one horrifically miserable, than to discover that there’s just a single happy organism on a planet? Certainly this doesn’t seem absurd or very repugnant. It being true isn’t a reason to abandon ethics!

I think our intuitions may be distorted by the excessive salience of the miserable people. Remember, in the world that the VRC says is better than the one full of happy people, basically 100% of people have good lives.

One can make this argument with even more modest premises. Imagine there was an alien planet. We learn either:

  1. It was full of aliens with barely worthwhile lives. There was a one in a trillion chance that it had someone with a very bad life.

  2. It had a one in a trillion chance that it had one person with a good life.

Intuitively, it seems plausible that 1 is better than 2. But if every planet is in state 1 rather than 2, then that means that there are a bunch of beings with horrible lives and a gargantuan number with lives barely worth living, instead of a bunch with great lives. This implies the very repugnant conclusion.

Argument 6 Debunking

Here is an explanation of why we find the very repugnant conclusion, well, very repugnant. Humans do not have reliable intuitions about large numbers. In experiments, people pay about as much to save 2,000 birds as to save 200,000 birds. As numbers get larger, our intuitions about the significance of the numbers don’t change. Even though 200,000 birds is 100x more than 2,000 birds, our brain registers both as [BIG NUMBER].

So here is an independently motivated and psychologically plausible account of where we go wrong: we intuitively underrate the goodness of large amounts of good stuff. Thus, we underestimate how good the world that has a bunch of people with barely worthwhile lives is, just like we underestimate how good it is to save 200,000 birds. This explains our error in the very repugnant conclusion case (see here for more discussion of this debunking account and its usefulness in explaining other sources of moral errors).

Argument 7 No plausible alternative

There are weird and gerrymandered ways out of the very repugnant conclusion. But at a high level, I think that there are only six main ways to go:

  1. Hold that no number of bad lives can be outweighed by any amount of welfare. More precisely, if there’s anyone with a bad life, the world is bad, no matter how much welfare it has.

  2. Hold that really horrible lives can’t be outweighed in badness by a large number of barely bad lives.

  3. Hold that it’s bad to create people with barely worthwhile lives. This badness can be weighed against the badness of torture. The two are commensurable.

  4. Hold that it’s bad to create people with welfare below some threshold. However, this is only a tiny bit bad, so no matter how much of it there is, it can’t be weighed against creating people with horrible lives.

  5. Hold that it’s good to create people with welfare below some threshold. However, it’s just barely good, so its goodness is not commensurable with creating people with a very high level of well-being.

  6. Hold that the value of creating people with welfare below some threshold is imprecise, so that it’s neither good nor bad, but it’s not that significant, so it can’t be weighed against creating people with great lives.

  7. Deny transitivity.

Here’s why that’s the basic lay of the land: denying 1-2 together imply that intense pain can be weighed against a high amount of well-being. Denying 1 implies that great lives can outweigh slightly negative lives. Denying 2 implies that enough slightly bad lives can outweigh terrible lives.

So all we need after that to establish the very repugnant conclusion is that a very large amount of well-being can be weighed against a large number of people with a small amount of well-being. For it not to be weighable, either a person being created with a good life would have to be bad, good but not weighable, or neither good nor bad but not weighable. Denying 3-4 covers the first possibility, denying 5 covers the second, denying 6 covers the last. Transitivity (implied by the denial of 7) implies that a chain A-N of things each weighable against the next successive item implies A is weighable against N, which implies the very repugnant conclusion in conjunction with 1-6.

So let’s see if those are plausible.

I find 1 crazy. If we discovered an alien planet where one alien had a slightly bad life, and everybody else had a great life, that would be good news. In fact, 1 seems way worse than the repugnant conclusion—it implies that a world full of happy people and one slightly miserable person is less good than one where there’s more total utility and everyone but one person has an amazing life, and that one life is slightly bad.

The falsity of 1 also follows from non-extreme priority. Suppose that there are a bunch of people with worthwhile lives. Imagine making one of them slightly worse off to make another trillion have amazing lives. Keep repeating that until the original one has a slightly bad life. At each step of the way, things are getting better. In the end, then, things are better. But if things are better in the end, then 1 is false.

Accepting 2 also seems bad to me. I’ve made this case in more detail here and here, but the basic idea: it’s very plausible that if you replace one person with a bad life with a trillion people with slightly less bad lives, things have gotten worse. But if you keep doing that over and over again, you’re left with lives that are just barely bad. In any case, even if you accept 2, you’ll still have to give up one of the self-evident-seeming premises in the Arrhenius proof.

Accepting 3 is one of the more attractive options. It’s called the critical level view. But it implies the sadistic conclusion. Flooding the world with people with barely worthwhile lives is worse than flooding it with a much smaller number of people being tortured. Surely no number of happy lizards basking in the sun is so bad as to be worse than Auschwitz. It doesn’t even seem bad.

Furthermore, I don’t really think it takes the sting out of the very repugnant conclusion. For one, the sadistic conclusion is the structural analogue of the very repugnant conclusion. The very repugnant conclusion says: a bunch of barely worthwhile lives can outweigh the badness of a smaller number of horrible lives.5 The sadistic conclusion says: the badness of a bunch of slightly worthwhile lives can outweigh the horribleness of a smaller number of people with horrible lives. Surely the sadistic conclusion is worse! Surely the conclusion “a bunch of slightly good lives can be arbitrarily good and outweigh really bad stuff” is less bad than “a bunch of slightly good lives can be arbitrarily bad, and be worse than really bad stuff!”

Similarly, this view implies an analogue of the repugnant conclusion. The thing that’s repugnant about the RC, intuitively, is the idea that though a life that’s barely worth living is just a little bit good, enough of them can be good to any arbitrary degree. We intuitively think that no matter how many small goods you get, they won’t be thaaaat good.

The critical level view defender simply relocates what a barely good life is. The view implies that for a life to be slightly good—in the sense that it makes the world a bit better—it has to be a pretty darn good life. But this still implies repugnance—a bunch of things that are just a tiny bit good are collectively good to an arbitrarily large degree.

I also think the critical level view just can’t possibly be right if morality is objective. The moral facts are supposed to precisely determine some non-zero welfare level. And only above that special level is your existence fortunate. This seems so arbitrary! It would be like if the fundamental mathematical facts contained unique reference to some specific number like 7.2.

Option 4 is “Hold that it’s bad to create people with welfare below some threshold. However, this is only a tiny bit bad, so no matter how much of it there is, it can’t be weighed against creating people with horrible lives.” This has the same problems as the critical level view, minus implying the sadistic conclusion. It also has the same problems as option 2. It must hold that there’s some threshold of misery, where no number of people even slightly below the threshold is as bad as a vastly smaller number slightly above the threshold.

Option 5 is “Hold that it’s good to create people with welfare below some threshold. However, it’s just barely good, so its goodness is not commensurable with creating people with a very high level of well-being.” First of all, either this view will have the same problem as views 2 and 4—implying that at some point slightly lowering intensity of suffering and increasing the number of victims by a quadrillion-fold doesn’t make things worse—or it will imply a puzzling asymmetry between positive and negative welfare.

After all, any version of this view that grants that increasing the number of victims can compensate for slight decreases in intensity will imply that a bunch of people with slightly bad lives is worse than a smaller number with horrendous lives. So if positive and negative welfare are treated similarly, any view that meets the criterion specified in the last sentence will imply the very repugnant conclusion.

This view is objectionably focused on the best. Suppose there were a bunch of people with barely worthwhile lives. Let’s call the first person Fred. Suppose you can either raise Fred’s welfare by 1 unit or raise a million people’s welfare by .5 units. It seems better to raise the million people’s welfare. Now, imagine you have that option again with a different group of a million—to raise their welfare by .5 units or to raise Fred’s welfare by 1 unit. Again, it seems better to raise their welfare by .5 units. However, this view requires preferring to benefit Fred. If you keep benefitting Fred, you can bring him over the threshold, so that his life is better than any number of people with barely worthwhile lives of .5 units of welfare.

Option 6 is: “Hold that the value of creating people with welfare below some threshold is imprecise, so that it’s neither good nor bad, but it’s not that significant, so it can’t be weighed against creating people with great lives.” This is, in essence, the critical range view.

First of all, this implies that there is imprecise value. But that is false (or so I say, anyways).

Second, so long as this view works symmetrically on the positive end and the negative end, it will violate the constraint that increasing the number of victims can compensate for slight decreases in intensity, making things overall worse. That is hard to believe.

Third, this violates non-elitism. If you lower a person’s welfare to be within the range, and then bump up other people to be at the higher end of the range, in the end, things will be incomparable—not better or equally good. Relatedly, if lives below some threshold are categorically less important than lives above some threshold, then raising one person’s welfare a tiny bit above the threshold is better than raising a bunch of people—trillions and trillions—to be slightly below the threshold. This is, again, hard to believe.

The last option is rejecting transitivity. Transitivity is the idea that if A>B and B>C, then A>C. I think rejecting intransitivity is very implausible—it just seems impossible, if you know what better means, for A to be better than B and B to be better than C, but for A to be worse than C. Plus I think transitivity is supported by very strong arguments. In addition, as Arrhenius writes:

However, as I have shown elsewhere, the axiological population theorems, including the above one, can be reconstructed on the normative level, in terms of what one ought to choose, without any appeal to transitivity (see Arrhenius 2004, 2011). Instead of a non-transitive ordering of populations, one gets a situation in which all of the available actions are forbidden, i.e., a moral dilemma. Hence, it does not look like we can exorcise the paradoxes of population ethics by giving up some formal condition like the transitivity of “better than”.

Conclusion

I accept the very repugnant conclusion. There are very strong arguments for accepting it and it isn’t that repugnant, in my view, when you think about it correctly. It is a suspicious fact that in every case outside of infinite ethics of seemingly intractable ethical paradox, one way out is to believe the thing that utilitarians believed all along. My preferred explanation is that this is because we’re right. Hopefully one day the very repugnant conclusion will be accepted by the world, and renamed the sunshine, lollipops, and rainbows conclusion.
